tracks.title: A disk that rides in the file
tracks.text: Lesson nine — the VFS. The virtual file system is the workbook's own disk. Real files and directories, SQLite-backed… riding inside the artifact. [curious] The workspace your code and your agents work in is the same file you can send. And nothing they do can touch the computer it's sitting on.

tracks.title: Where does an agent keep files?
tracks.text: Give software somewhere to work, and you've answered most of what it needs. The industry's answer for agents has been one of two bad options. Option one: hand over your real disk. Your keychain… your documents… everything a bad instruction can reach. Option two: rent a computer in the cloud, metered by the second — so the agent has a scratch directory that evaporates when the meter stops. [curious] Both answers share an assumption worth questioning… that a file system has to belong to a machine. Yours, or someone else's. But the amount of disk a project actually needs is small. And what it needs from that disk is mundane. Paths… directories… read, write, list. Nothing about that requires an operating system underneath. [excited] It just requires somewhere structured for bytes to live.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The VFS is the workbook's own disk. A virtual file system — real files and directories, SQLite-backed — riding inside the artifact. Readable and writable by the workbook's code and agents… and sealed off from the host machine, by construction. It's the third layer of the workbook anatomy. The interface up front… WebAssembly for compute… and underneath them, a disk. [curious] So the file doesn't just describe a piece of software. It contains the place where that software keeps its things.

tracks.title: A disk you can query
tracks.text: Under the paths, the VFS is tables. And that duality is the feature. To the code, it's a disk — open, read, write, list, like any file system. To a query, it's SQLite — the same bytes, askable. [curious] Most file systems make you choose… easy paths, or real queries. Because this one is a database wearing a directory tree, the questions that are painful on a normal disk become single statements. Everything modified since the last deploy. Every file over a megabyte. Every note the agent touched this week. [chuckles] Your disk speaks SQL.

tracks.title: Two readings, again
tracks.text: The workbook lesson describes one file with two readings — a document to a human, a container to an engine. The VFS is where that duality becomes concrete. Opened in a browser… the VFS loads into memory. Code reads and writes it for real — a game saves, a dashboard filters, an agent's notes are right there. And when you close the tab, the file on your disk is exactly what it was. The artifact stays honest. Viewing never mutates. [curious] Docked into a Nexus… the same VFS becomes the workbook's live disk. Persistent. Synced. Served. Writes survive restarts… schedules write into it overnight… and the copy you serve to a thousand people reads from it. Same paths. Same queries. Same code. [excited] The only thing that changed is that the disk now has a heartbeat.

tracks.title: The workspace is the artifact
tracks.text: Here's the consequence that makes this construct worth its own lesson. An agent's working directory — its notes, its drafts, its intermediate data, its memory — lives in the VFS of the workbook it's tending. Which means the workspace, and the work product… are the same object. [curious] Hand someone the file, and you've handed them the project. The app… its data… and the entire working state of the crew that built it. No zipping up a folder. No it-works-on-my-sandbox. [excited] The thing you collaborate on and the thing you ship… stopped being different things.

tracks.title: Why this is the safe shape
tracks.text: An agent that needs your file system is an agent you have to trust with your file system. An agent whose entire disk is the workbook's VFS needs no trust at all. There is nothing else its writes can reach. Not your documents. Not your keychain. Not a stray credentials file. The security model's grants-not-inheritance rule starts here — the default disk is the one riding in the artifact… and everything beyond it is a specific, revocable permission. [curious] This is also why the blast radius stays boring. A confused agent can trash exactly one VFS. Which is versioned… diffable… and restorable. [chuckles] Because it's inside a file that git has been tracking all along.

tracks.title: Where the disk ends
tracks.text: Honesty section. The VFS is a project-scale disk… not a media vault. SQLite holds gigabytes comfortably, but a workbook stays pleasant to share in the tens of megabytes — so heavy assets belong behind an engine, with the workbook querying them. And in a browser, persistence is the file's. Changes live in memory until you save, or dock. The open tab is a reading room… not a writing desk. [curious] For durability, schedules, and serving — the engine is the answer. The way it always is, for the living part.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Are they real files, or files in quotation marks? Real, to everything inside. Code opens paths… agents list directories… tools read and write bytes. The quotation marks only appear from the host machine's point of view. Which is exactly the point. Your OS sees one file. The workbook sees a disk. Can I get files out? Always. Unbundle the workbook, and the tree unpacks to ordinary files. The disk travels with the file — it's never trapped in it. What about two people writing at once? That's a docked question. Through a Nexus, the engine holds the live VFS and serializes the writes. [curious] And why SQLite underneath? Same reason as the rest of the anatomy. No invented formats. The most deployed database on earth… doing what existing ingredients do when they share a file.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's the VFS. A real disk, riding in the artifact — queryable like a database, sealed off from the host, and identical in the browser and on the engine. [curious] The workspace is the work product. That idea echoes through every other lesson… [excited] go meet its neighbors.
